Main.sentence: Anwar Nasser Abdulla al-Awlaki ( ___E:Arabic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language)___ : أنور العولقي , romanized: Anwar al-'Awlaqī ; April 21, 1971 – September 30, 2011) was an American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer assassinated ___E:in Yemen in 2011 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_strikes_in_Yemen)___ by a U.S. ___E:drone strike U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_strike)___ ordered by President ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ .
Al-Awlaki was the first U.S. citizen to be targeted and assassinated by a U.S. government drone strike.

U.S. government officials alleged that al-Awlaki, a ___E:dual citizen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dual_citizen)___ of the U.S. and Yemen, was a key organizer for the Islamist militant group ___E:al-Qaeda U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda)___ .
Al-Awlaki was born in ___E:Las Cruces, New Mexico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Cruces,_New_Mexico)___ , U.S., in 1971 to parents from Yemen.
Growing up partly in the United States and partly in Yemen, he attended various U.S. universities in the 1990s and early 2000s.
He also worked as an ___E:imam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imam)___ despite having no religious qualifications and almost no religious education.
Al-Awlaki returned to Yemen in early 2004 and became a university lecturer  after a brief stint as a public speaker in the United Kingdom.
He was detained by Yemeni authorities in 2006 and spent 18 months in prison  before being released without facing trial.

Following his release from Yemeni custody, Al-Awlaki had significantly ___E:radicalized U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radicalization)___ , and began to speak overtly in support of violence, also condemning the U.S. government's foreign policy towards Muslims.

He was linked to ___E:Nidal Hasan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nidal_Hasan)___ , the convicted perpetrator of the ___E:2009 Fort Hood shooting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Fort_Hood_shooting)___ , and ___E:Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar_Farouk_Abdulmutallab)___ , who attempted to detonate a bomb on ___E:Northwest Airlines Flight 253 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Airlines_Flight_253)___ .
The Yemeni government tried al-Awlaki in absentia in November 2010 for plotting to kill foreigners and being a member of al-Qaeda.
A Yemeni judge ordered that he be captured "dead or alive".
U.S. officials said that in 2009, al-Awlaki was promoted to the rank of "regional commander" within al-Qaeda.
He repeatedly called for jihad against the United States.
In April 2010, al-Awlaki was placed on a ___E:CIA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency)___ ___E:kill list U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_list)___ by President Obama.
Al-Awlaki's father and ___E:civil rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights)___ groups challenged the order in court.

The U.S. deployed ___E:unmanned aircraft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmanned_aerial_vehicle)___ (drones) in Yemen to search for and kill him,  firing at and failing to kill him at least once.  Al-Awlaki was killed on September 30, 2011.

In June 2014, a previously classified memorandum from the ___E:U.S. Department of Justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Department_of_Justice)___ was released; the memorandum described al-Awlaki's killing as a lawful act of war.  Civil liberties advocates have called the killing of al-Awlaki an extrajudicial execution that breached al-Awlaki's constitutional rights.

The New York Times wrote in 2015 that al-Awlaki's public statements and videos had been more influential in inspiring acts of ___E:Islamic terrorism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_terrorism)___ in the wake of his killing than they were before his death.

Anwar al-Awlaki was born in ___E:Las Cruces, New Mexico U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Cruces,_New_Mexico)___ , in 1971 to parents from Yemen, while his father, ___E:Nasser al-Awlaki U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasser_al-Awlaki)___ , was doing graduate work at U.S. universities.

His father was a ___E:Fulbright Scholar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulbright_Scholar)___  who earned a master's degree in agricultural economics at ___E:New Mexico State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico_State_University)___ in 1971, received a doctorate at the ___E:University of Nebraska–Lincoln U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nebraska%E2%80%93Lincoln)___ , and worked at the ___E:University of Minnesota U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Minnesota)___ from 1975 to 1977.   Nasser al-Awlaki served as Agriculture Minister in ___E:Ali Abdullah Saleh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Abdullah_Saleh)___ 's government.
He was also President of ___E:Sana'a University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sana%27a_University)___ .

Yemen's ___E:prime minister U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Yemen)___ from 2007 to 2011, ___E:Ali Mohammed Mujur U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_Mohammed_Mujur)___ , was a relative.
The family returned to Yemen in 1978, when al-Awlaki was seven years old.   He lived there for 11 years, and studied at Azal Modern School.
Around 1990, al-Awlaki went to the U.S. to attend college.

He earned a ___E:B.S. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science)___ in ___E:civil engineering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_engineering)___ from ___E:Colorado State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_State_University)___ (1994), where he was president of the ___E:Muslim Student Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Student_Association)___ .

In 1993, while still a college student in Colorado State's civil engineering program, al-Awlaki visited ___E:Afghanistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan)___ in the aftermath of the ___E:Soviet occupation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War)___ .
He spent some time training with the mujahideen who had fought the Soviets.

He was depressed by the country's poverty and hunger, and "wouldn't have gone with al-Qaeda," according to friends from Colorado State, who said he was profoundly affected by the trip.    ___E:Mullah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mullah)___ ___E:Mohammed Omar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mullah_Omar)___ did not form the ___E:Taliban U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taliban)___ until 1994. When Al-Awlaki returned to campus, he showed increased interest in religion and politics.

Al-Awlaki studied ___E:Education Leadership U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_studies)___ at ___E:San Diego State University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_State_University)___ , earning a master's degree.

He worked on a doctorate in Human Resource Development at ___E:The George Washington University Graduate School of Education and Human Development U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_George_Washington_University_Graduate_School_of_Education_and_Human_Development)___ in 2001.

In 1994, al-Awlaki ___E:married a cousin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cousin_marriage)___ from Yemen,  and began service as a part-time ___E:imam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imam)___ of the Denver Islamic Society.
In 1996, he was chastised by an elder for encouraging a Saudi student to ___E:fight in Chechnya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Chechen_War)___ against the Russians.
He left Denver soon after, moving to San Diego.

From 1996 to 2000, al-Awlaki was imam of the Masjid Ar-Ribat al-Islami mosque in ___E:San Diego U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego)___ , California, where he had a following of 200–300 people.

U.S. officials later alleged that ___E:Nawaf al-Hazmi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawaf_al-Hazmi)___ and ___E:Khalid al-Mihdhar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_al-Mihdhar)___ , hijackers of ___E:American Airlines Flight 77 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines_Flight_77)___ , attended his sermons and personally met him during this period, although Al-Awlaki told authorities their conversations were trivial in nature.
Hazmi later lived in ___E:Northern Virginia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Virginia)___ and attended al-Awlaki's mosque there.
The 9/11 Commission Report said that the hijackers "reportedly respected [al-Awlaki] as a religious figure".
While in San Diego, al-Awlaki volunteered with youth organizations, fished, discussed his travels with friends, and created a popular and lucrative series of recorded lectures.
In 1998 and 1999, he served as vice-president for the ___E:Charitable Society for Social Welfare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charitable_Society_for_Social_Welfare)___ .

Although the FBI investigated al-Awlaki from June 1999 through March 2000 for possible links to ___E:Hamas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamas)___ , the Bin Laden contact ___E:Ziyad Khaleel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziyad_Khaleel)___ , and a visit by an associate of ___E:Omar Abdel Rahman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omar_Abdel_Rahman)___ ,  it did not find sufficient evidence for a criminal prosecution.
In 2004, the ___E:FBI U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation)___ described this group as a "front organization to funnel money to terrorists".

Al-Awlaki told reporters that he resigned from leading the San Diego mosque "after an uneventful four years," and took a brief ___E:sabbatical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabbatical)___ , traveling overseas to various countries.

Al-Awlaki decided to pursue his PhD and was accepted at ___E:George Washington University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_University)___ in Washington, D.C., and was soon recruited to be the imam of the nearby suburban ___E:Dar al-Hijrah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dar_al-Hijrah)___ mosque in 2000.  One of the mosque's board members who hired Al-Awlaki stated he was convinced that al-Awlaki had no inclinations or activities to do with terrorism.
The new imam, who was described as alluring and charming at this time,  began to draw young people to Dar Al-Hijrah  while connecting with the sophisticated Muslim community of Northern Virginia.

His proficiency as a public speaker and command of the English language helped him attract followers who did not speak Arabic. "He was the magic bullet", according to the mosque spokesman ___E:Johari Abdul-Malik U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johari_Abdul-Malik)___ . "He had everything all in a box."  Al-Awlaki was considered a moderate during his time at Dar Al-Hijrah, publicly condemned the ___E:September 11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ and ___E:Al-Qaeda U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda)___ , was even invited to speak at the ___E:United States Department of Defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense)___  and became the first imam to conduct a prayer service for the ___E:Congressional Muslim Staffer Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Muslim_Staffer_Association)___ at the ___E:U.S. Capitol U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Capitol)___ .
He led academic discussions frequented by FBI Director of Counter-Intelligence for the Middle East ___E:Gordon M. Snow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_M._Snow)___ .

Al-Awlaki also served as the Muslim ___E:chaplain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaplain)___ at ___E:George Washington University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_University)___ .
Soon after the 9/11 attacks, al-Awlaki was sought in Washington, D.C., by the media to answer questions about Islam, its rituals, and its relation to the attacks.
He was interviewed by National Geographic ,  The New York Times , and other media.
Al-Awlaki condemned the attacks.

According to an ___E:NPR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR)___ report in 2010, in 2001 al-Awlaki appeared to be a moderate who could "bridge the gap between the United States and the worldwide community of Muslims."  The New York Times said at the time that he was "held up as a new generation of Muslim leader capable of merging East and West."  In 2010, ___E:Fox News U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News)___ and the New York Daily News reported that some months after the 9/11 attacks, a Pentagon employee invited al-Awlaki to a luncheon in the Secretary's Office of General Counsel.

The U.S. ___E:secretary of the Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Army)___ had suggested that a ___E:moderate Muslim U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderate_Muslim)___ be invited to give a talk.
There is no way that the people who did this could be Muslim, and if they claim to be Muslim, then they have perverted their religion.

Al-Awlaki appeared on law enforcement's radars when federal investigators discovered two of the alleged 9/11 hijackers had attended the same mosque in San Diego during the same time Al-Awlaki served as imam, as well as Dar Al-Hijrah (along with a third alleged hijacker).

When police investigating the 9/11 attacks raided the ___E:Hamburg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg)___ apartment of ___E:Ramzi bin al-Shibh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramzi_bin_al-Shibh)___ , they found the telephone number of al-Awlaki among bin al-Shibh's personal contacts.

Six days after the 9/11 attacks, al-Awlaki ___E:suggested U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9/11_Truth_movement)___ in writing on the IslamOnline.net website that Israeli intelligence agents might have been responsible for the attacks, and that the FBI "went into the roster of the airplanes, and whoever has a Muslim or Arab name became the hijacker by default".
The FBI interviewed al-Awlaki four times in the eight days following the 9/11 attacks.
FBI agents conducted repeated interviews and placed the imam under surveillance.

Although some law enforcement and public officials have been outspoken about their suspicions of Al-Awlaki's role in the 9/11 plot,   no solid evidence emerged linking him to the plot.  Al-Awlaki resigned from Dar Al-Hijrah in early 2002 due to post-9/11 media attention that distracted the imam from his duties, according to the mosque's outreach director.

Later in 2002, al-Awlaki posted an essay in Arabic on the Islam Today website titled "Why Muslims Love Death", lauding the fervor of Palestinian ___E:suicide bombers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_bomber)___ .

He expressed a similar opinion in a speech at a London mosque later that year.   By July 2002, al-Awlaki was under investigation in the United States for having received money from the subject of a U.S. ___E:Joint Terrorism Task Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Terrorism_Task_Force)___ investigation.
His name was added to the list of terrorism suspects.

In June 2002, a Denver federal judge signed an ___E:arrest warrant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrest_warrant)___ for al-Awlaki for ___E:passport fraud U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passport_fraud)___ .

On October 9, the Denver ___E:U.S. Attorney's Office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Attorney%27s_Office)___ filed a motion to dismiss the complaint and ___E:vacate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacate)___ the arrest warrant.
Prosecutors believed that they lacked sufficient evidence of a crime, according to U.S.
Attorney Dave Gaouette, who authorized its withdrawal.

Al-Awlaki had listed Yemen rather than the United States as his place of birth on his 1990 application for a U.S. ___E:Social Security number U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_number)___ , soon after arriving in the US.  Al-Awlaki used this documentation to obtain a passport in 1993. He later corrected his place of birth to Las Cruces, New Mexico.   "The bizarre thing is if you put Yemen down (on the application), it would be harder to get a Social Security number than to say you are a native-born citizen of ___E:Las Cruces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Cruces,_New_Mexico)___ ", Gaouette said.

Prosecutors could not charge him in October 2002, when he returned from a trip abroad, because a 10-year ___E:statute of limitations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_limitations)___ on lying to the ___E:Social Security Administration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_Administration)___ had expired.

According to a 2012 investigative report by ___E:Fox News U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_News)___ , the arrest warrant for passport fraud was still in effect on the morning of October 10, 2002, when FBI Agent Wade Ammerman ordered al-Awlaki's release.

U.S. congressman ___E:Frank Wolf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Wolf_(politician))___ (R-VA) and several congressional committees urged FBI Director ___E:Robert Mueller U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mueller)___ to provide an explanation about the bureau's interactions with al-Awlaki, including why he was released from federal custody when there was an outstanding warrant for his arrest.
The motion for rescinding the arrest warrant was approved by a magistrate judge on October 10 and filed on October 11.
ABC News reported in 2009 that the Joint Terrorism Task Force in San Diego disagreed with the decision to cancel the warrant.
They were monitoring al-Awlaki and wanted to "look at him under a microscope".
But U.S.

Attorney Gaouette said that no objection had been raised to the rescinding of the warrant during a meeting that included Ray Fournier, the San Diego federal diplomatic security agent whose allegation had set in motion the effort to obtain a warrant.
Gaouette said that if al-Awlaki had been convicted at the time, he would have faced about six months in custody.
The New York Times suggested later that al-Awlaki had claimed birth in Yemen (his family's place of origin) to qualify for scholarship money granted to foreign citizens.

U.S. congressman ___E:Frank R. Wolf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_R._Wolf)___ (R-VA) wrote in May 2010 that by claiming to be foreign-born, al-Awlaki fraudulently obtained more than $20,000 in scholarship funds reserved for foreign students.
While living in Northern Virginia, al-Awlaki visited ___E:Ali al-Timimi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_al-Timimi)___ , later known as a radical Islamic cleric.

Al-Timimi was convicted in 2005 and is now serving a life sentence for leading the ___E:Virginia Jihad Network U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Jihad_Network)___ , inciting Muslim followers to fight with the ___E:Taliban U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taliban)___ against the US.

Al-Awlaki left the United States before the end of 2002, because of a "climate of fear and intimidation" according to Imam ___E:Johari Abdul-Malik U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johari_Abdul-Malik)___ of the Dar al-Hijrah mosque.
He lived in the UK for several months, where he gave talks attended by up to 200 people.
He urged young Muslim followers: "The important lesson to learn here is never, ever trust the kuffar [disbeliever].
Do not trust them! [Their leaders] are plotting to kill this religion.
They're plotting night and day."  "He was the main man who translated the jihad into English," said a student who attended his lectures in 2003.

He gave a series of lectures in December 2002 and January 2003 at the London Masjid al-Tawhid mosque, describing the rewards martyrs ( ___E:Shahid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shahid)___ ) receive in paradise ( ___E:Jannah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jannah)___ ).

He began to gain supporters, particularly among young Muslims,  and undertook a lecture tour of England and Scotland in 2002 in conjunction with the ___E:Muslim Association of Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Association_of_Britain)___ .
He also lectured at "ExpoIslamia", an event held by ___E:Islamic Forum Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Forum_Europe)___ .

At the ___E:East London Mosque U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_London_Mosque)___ he told his audience: "A Muslim is a brother of a Muslim... he does not betray him, and he does not hand him over...
You don't hand over a Muslim to the enemies."

In the UK's ___E:Parliament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom)___ in 2003, ___E:Louise Ellman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Ellman)___ , ___E:MP U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament)___ for ___E:Liverpool Riverside U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Riverside)___ , discussed the relationship between al-Awlaki and the ___E:Muslim Association of Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Association_of_Britain)___ , a ___E:Muslim Brotherhood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Brotherhood)___ front organization founded by ___E:Kemal el-Helbawy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kemal_el-Helbawy&action=edit&redlink=1)___ , a senior member of the ___E:Egyptian Muslim Brotherhood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian_Muslim_Brotherhood)___ .
Al-Awlaki returned to Yemen in early 2004, where he lived in ___E:Shabwah Governorate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabwah_Governorate)___ with his wife and five children.
He lectured at ___E:Iman University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iman_University)___ , headed by ___E:Abdul Majeed al-Zindani U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdul_Majeed_al-Zindani)___ .

The latter has been included on the ___E:UN 1267 Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISIL_(Da%27esh)_and_Al-Qaida_Sanctions_Committee)___ 's list of individuals belonging to or associated with al-Qaeda.
Al-Zindani denied having any influence over al-Awlaki, or that he had been his "direct teacher".
Some believe [who?] that the school's curriculum deals mostly, if not exclusively, with radical Islamic studies, and promotes radicalism.
American convert ___E:John Walker Lindh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Walker_Lindh)___ and other alumni have been associated with militant groups.
On August 31, 2006, al-Awlaki was arrested with four others on charges of kidnapping a Shiite teenager for ransom, and participating in an al-Qaeda plot to kidnap a U.S. military attaché.

He was imprisoned in 2006 and 2007.  He was interviewed around September 2007 by two FBI agents with regard to the 9/11 attacks and other subjects. ___E:John Negroponte U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Negroponte)___ , the U.S. ___E:Director of National Intelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_National_Intelligence)___ , told Yemeni officials he did not object to al-Awlaki's detention.
His name was on a list of 100 prisoners whose release was sought by al-Qaeda-linked militants in Yemen.
After 18 months in a Yemeni prison, al-Awlaki was released on December 12, 2007, following the intercession of his tribe.
According to a Yemeni security official, he was released because he had repented.
He moved to his family home in Saeed, a hamlet in the Shabwa mountains.

___E:Moazzam Begg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moazzam_Begg)___ 's ___E:Cageprisoners U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cageprisoners)___ , an organization representing former ___E:Guantanamo detainees U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guantanamo_detainee)___ , campaigned for al-Awlaki's release when he was in prison in Yemen.
Al-Awlaki told Begg in an interview shortly after his release that prior to his incarceration in Yemen, he had condemned the 9/11 attacks.
In December 2008, al-Awlaki sent a communique to the Somali militant group, ___E:al-Shabaab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harakat_al-Shabaab_Mujahideen)___ , congratulating them.
"He's the most dangerous man in Yemen.
He's intelligent, sophisticated, Internet-savvy, and very charismatic.
He can sell anything to anyone, and right now he's selling jihad ".
Al-Awlaki provided al-Qaeda members in Yemen with the protection of his powerful tribe, the Awlakis, against the government.
The tribal code required it to protect those who seek refuge and assistance.
This imperative has greater force when the person is a member of the tribe or a tribesman's friend.
The tribe's motto is "We are the sparks of Hell; whoever interferes with us will be burned."  Al-Awlaki also reportedly helped negotiate deals with leaders of other tribes.
Sought by Yemeni authorities who were investigating his al-Qaeda ties, al-Awlaki went into hiding in approximately March 2009, according to his father.

By December 2009, al-Awlaki was on the Yemeni government's most-wanted list.  He was believed to be hiding in Yemen's ___E:Shabwa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shabwah_Governorate)___ or ___E:Mareb U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma%27rib_Governorate)___ regions, which are part of the so-called "triangle of evil".
The area has attracted al-Qaeda militants, who seek refuge among local tribes unhappy with Yemen's central government.
